Use the VA service., They have people who make resumes for you.

I used them when I first got out.

Your resume is about selling 'You' to strangers. Make a nice little letterhead with your name, address, and your contact information.

If you did ANYTHING in the military that you could suggest helps you at this job, jot it down - you can weed out the irrelevant stuff later.

Invest in some good paper. No need to go out and buy woven linen sheets - but something thicker than 20lb printer paper. If you can see the shadow of your hand/color of the table through it, it's too thin. (If you're printing at home, there's stuff marketed as 'resume paper' but it looks marbled and is crazy ass expensive. I don't care for it, but it's your resume.) It's not about looking like you have money, it's about showing how seriously you're prepared to take the job. Makes it look like you gave it that little bit of extra.

If you're a vet, contact the VA about Career Centers and any job assistance programs. They aren't all about finding you jobs (although some do that too). They're there to help people just like you who have marketable skills but don't know how to market - you want to work, not schmooze. They have little get togethers that talk about making a resume (or they just help you make them), they go over interview etiquette (what to wear, what questions to expect and how best to answer them, key phrases to use to promote yourself, etc), and sometimes they'll have little trial runs to help get your nerves under control. You have this resource, so use the fuck out of it. Your taxes are paying for it.

Check your local job assistance places and career centers, they usually have resume builders too and, if you don't want to go get them printed and don't have a printer at home, they'll usually give you a minimum of three resumes and a folder to keep them in. Lots of programs to help you there too. Usually.

Get ready to talk pretty. You didn't clean the shitter, you assisted with waste management. You didn't run drills, you participated in team building activities. Cleaned your gun every day? Washed trucks? Nope - 'Maintained personal/public equipment daily to keep it in the best working order.' A good resume won't make people go 'yikes, sounds rough' - it'll make them go 'hm. i think HR said something about that at the last meeting'. You aren't lying, you're making your experience PC and relevant to the job you're applying for. When asked about it during an interview, you can back it up honestly. Be proud of what you accomplished. Be confident. The VA rep might be the best person to help with that - chances are a lot of people are in the same boat as you. You're qualified to do the job, you just need to sell your skills.

Some rules of the resume have changed, but if you don't have a lot of work history you're probably okay:

Try to keep body text around 12 pt font. Stick with Times New Roman, Arial, or Courier.

Keep copies of your resume on you and also on a flash drive. The person you sent your resume to may not be who interviews you. Walk in with a folder - have a notebook for jotting down your own personal notes (you professional, you!), a pen that FUCKING WORKS (omg, so embarrassing...), and a copy of your resume and references. Nothing looks slicker than your interviewer saying 'I'm sorry, you uploaded your resume and this isn't my computer' or 'I didn't get a copy of your resume from HR' - and you reach into the file and say 'Don't worry, sir/ma'am - I have a copy right here.' Smooth. Like a boss. Don't need it? Eh - you were prepared. They like that too.

Some people say to keep it to one page, but it's not a must anymore. Sell yourself on the first page - your contact info, your strengths/skills, any additional schooling you might have that is relevant to the job, and your Veteran Buff. I would also suggest your most recent outside-the-military job, but if you went in right after highschool you might not want to bother. You want it to be relevant to this job and saying you went into the military right out of highschool and made it your career is a pretty big buff.

Make a separate page for references.

Write a cover letter. Ain't gotta be long. Just like 'Dear sir/madam, thank you for taking the time to consider me.' Mention that you would appreciate the opportunity to discuss how you could be an asset to their company. Thank them, boom - cover letter. Again, it is about showing you are willing to put forth effort for them. You can find some great and simple examples on any search engine image search.

One page, no fluff, just the facts, no exceptions. Do not waste your potential employers' time. Tell your story in person (or over the phone if that's your first interview). This approach has worked excellently for me.

These are your categories, in this order:

Contact info - Name, email, phone #. Some people put their address, I do not. This is the only section you don't title, This section is the title.

Education - Include dates. If you have a degree, don't put your high school. If not, put your high school. If, in preparation for this job you are applying for you've taken courses, seminars, or whatever, you can include those, but only if they are relevant and only if you have completed them and can prove it.

Work Experience - In reverse chronological order, most recent to oldest. Include everything, especially if you have a reference. Include dates. I don't know how this would work exactly with a military past, but you can figure something out.

Certifications/Licenses/Awards/Comendations - In reverse chronological order, most recent to oldest. Include dates. Stay relevant.

Skills - I sort mine into 2 groups: Computer Skills and Physical Skills (I worked in architecture so my physical skills were things like drafting, model making, surveying. No one cares how fast you can run a mile, stay relevant). Since you're going to a factory job and you have a military background, include skills that you honed while serving that are relevant for the position you want. Relevant skills you developed in high school are good too. You can put hobby-level skills here only if they are relevant. Remember, no fluff.

That's it for the resume. Do not include references on your resume, bring them to interviews on a separate sheet of paper. Why? Because it is critical that you represent yourself to your potential employers before they have a chance to call one your references. You need to make your own first impression. Also, do not hand your references to your interviewers until the end of the interview. Protect that list. Only give it out if the interview went well and you really want the job. Also, instead of asking your interviewers if they want references, say "I brought a list of references" and just hand it over. Never ask for permission to give over the list.

PROOFREAD OVER AND OVER AND OVER AND OVER. One typo is all it takes to land your resume in the trash.

Look at other resumes and use a resume builder program or template like in ms word. Try to keep it to one page, use short phrases instead of sentences. Sometimes we who hire only have 5 minutes to pull resumes from a stack to fill one position, and we don't always get through all the candidates. If your resume is long, it'll probably be put to the side for "read if I got time later". Short, one page and punchy sentences like

"awarded service commendation." "2 years medical training" "6 months in community outreach program"

Those stand out. Long flows sentences do not, and we think you can't get to the point, and can't work in a faster paced business environment.
Don't lie unless it's something that you can make a truth in a very short unexpected time frame.

Use action words to describe what you did for a company and keep them all in the past tense unless currently performing the function.

Organized, maintained, spearheaded, managed, distributed, specialized, and implemented are some good ones to start off with.
Make sure to put in your volunteer work, anything that can even be considered volunteer work.
